title: Basingstoke's long-lost haunted pub, and eight more spine-tingling ghost stories
excerpt: Explore Basingstoke’s most haunted places, from South View Cemetery and Basing House to The Haymarket, with ghost stories, apparitions and eerie legends.
content:
SCREAMS from the grave, phantom footsteps and objects apparently moving by themselves are among the eerie tales attached to some of Basingstoke's best-known locations.

With Halloween approaching, the town has no shortage of ghost stories for anyone brave enough to go looking for them.

Some stem from genuine pieces of Basingstoke's history which have acquired supernatural legends over generations, while others involve strange experiences reportedly witnessed by people living and working in the town.

From the tragic story of a woman supposedly buried alive to reported apparitions at Basing House, these are some of the places said to be among Basingstoke's most haunted.

The Holy Ghost Ruins

Perhaps Basingstoke's most gruesome tale is that of Alice Blunden, who was not buried alive once, but twice.

After falling unconscious in July 1674, reportedly after drinking poppy water, she was pronounced dead and buried at what is now South View Cemetery.

Children later claimed they could hear screams and groans coming from beneath the ground. When the coffin was eventually opened, Mrs Blunden was reportedly found alive, battered and bloodied after attempting to escape.

She was placed back in the grave with a guard supposed to watch over her, but after another night she was found dead, having apparently regained consciousness once again and struggled inside the coffin.

The story became one of Basingstoke's most notorious historic tales and is commemorated by a plaque at South View Cemetery.

A painting of The Barge area and the Reformers tree (Image: Neil Jepson)

Old Barge Inn

One of Basingstoke's long-lost pubs apparently had a resident who was reluctant to leave.

In 1968, the Hants & Berks Gazette reported on ghostly goings-on at the Old Barge Inn as the historic building was being stripped of its roof tiles, bricks and timbers before demolition.

According to the newspaper, a centuries-old story claimed the pub was haunted by the ghost of a bargeman's daughter who had been killed by a bargeman.

People connected with the pub reported hearing unexplained footsteps and other noises inside the building, while one account described the sound of something being thrown around upstairs when nobody could be found there.

The supposedly haunted building was also associated with sightings of a mysterious figure and the sound of walking and chains.

But as the Old Barge itself disappeared, apparently so did its ghost.

The 1968 Gazette proclaimed that after generations of local stories, “the ghost of Basingstoke's old Barge walks no more”.

The Woman in Grey

Cliddesden Road also has its own ghostly resident, according to local legend.

The former Shrubbery Maternity Home was reportedly haunted by an apparition known as the Woman in Grey.

Stories claimed that the mysterious figure would walk through the building, trying door handles and apparently checking on mothers and their babies.

The apparition has been linked in folklore to Jane Covey, the wife of a former owner, who died in 1851.

English Civil War reenactors at Basing House in 2018

Basing House

With centuries of dramatic history behind it, perhaps it is unsurprising that Basing House has acquired a few ghost stories of its own.

The Old Basing site endured a series of sieges during the English Civil War before finally falling to Parliamentary forces under Oliver Cromwell in 1645.

The ruins have subsequently become associated with supernatural stories, including claims that Cromwell himself has been seen at the site.

Ghost hunts have taken place there over the years, with visitors reporting unexplained shadows and other unusual experiences.

Whether Cromwell really decided to hang around after destroying the place is, of course, rather harder to establish.

The Haymarket theater on Wote Street.

The Haymarket

Thousands of people have passed through The Haymarket over the years, but stories suggest not every visitor has necessarily bought a ticket.

The Basingstoke theatre has been associated with tales of a mysterious figure appearing inside the auditorium.

Reported sightings have even taken place during daylight hours.

Warton Road Basingstoke (Image: Google Street View)

Warton Road

A property in Warton Road, South View, became associated with claims of apparent poltergeist activity.

Stories centred on objects supposedly moving and items mysteriously appearing with no obvious explanation.

As with many of Basingstoke's supernatural stories, exactly what lay behind the reports remains something of a mystery.

Park Prewett

Today's Limes Park looks very different from the site which occupied the area for much of the 20th century.

Park Prewett Hospital operated there between 1917 and 1997 before the land was ultimately redeveloped.

Across the decades, the former hospital became associated with reports of unexplained sightings and ghostly figures.

Much of the old site has since disappeared beneath the modern development, although pieces of its history remain visible.

And, if the stories are to be believed, perhaps some former occupants never entirely left.

The Rose and Crown circa 1950 (Photo by Alastair Blair)

The Rose and Crown

Another of Basingstoke's long-demolished pubs apparently came with its own unexplained noises.

During the 1960s, reports emerged of unusual sounds at the former Rose and Crown in Church Street.

The claims were sufficiently noteworthy to make it into the pages of the Hants & Berks Gazette, as this newspaper was then known.

The building was later demolished, taking whatever explanation there might have been for its strange noises with it.

Chequers Road (Image: Google Street View)

The mysterious truncheon of Chequers Road

One of Basingstoke's more unusual modern ghost stories emerged as recently as 2018.

The Gazette reported how a builder renovating a property in Chequers Road discovered a mysterious wooden object concealed inside a crevice.

The object was taken home so it could be identified before being returned the following day.

It was subsequently discovered to be an old Victorian police truncheon.

But according to the story, taking it away from the house appeared to have consequences.

The builder reportedly noticed an oppressive atmosphere at home before loud banging was heard in the kitchen that night.

Nothing could be found to explain the noise.

Later, the builder and his partner claimed they were woken by more banging, this time apparently coming from their bedroom door.

Again, there was no obvious source.

According to the account, the builder eventually announced that the truncheon would be taken straight back to where it had been found.

The noises then stopped.

The Victorian object was duly returned to the Chequers Road property the following day, with no further unexplained incidents reported.

Whether Basingstoke really is populated by phantom theatre-goers, Civil War ghosts and noisy Victorian police equipment is open to debate.
